title: Agents & Claude Code
scopeHtml: Scope: workflow vs agent, the three wiring paths, human-in-the-loop placement, Claude Code permission modes and settings, CLAUDE.md, rules, hooks, subagents and plugins.

notes.title: Workflow or agent
notes.html:
The first design decision. Choosing the wrong pattern at the start is the most expensive mistake in agent development. Using an agent where a workflow suffices adds behavioural complexity with no new capability. Using a workflow where an agent is needed produces a system that breaks whenever input deviates from the predetermined path.

Definitions. A workflow runs steps you wrote in code. An agent is a multi-step tool-use loop with managed context and a defined goal, where the model decides the path. Agents carry coordination overhead, expanded context costs and more surface area for failure.

Choose a workflow when… Choose an agent when…
you can enumerate the exact steps in code you can specify the goal and the tools but not the exact path
error cost is real and step-level guardrails matter the path through the work cannot be enumerated in advance
observability with standard tooling is required non-determinism is acceptable and actions are constrained by the registered toolset
inputs are well-constrained to a known set user inputs vary unpredictably in content and structure
every execution follows the same sequence the task needs creative sequencing of available tools

What you take on with an agent. The path emerges from the model's reasoning over accumulated context rather than explicit branching; observability needs transcript-level tooling rather than standard operational logging.

The progression. Start with the simplest pattern that solves the problem: a single API call, then a workflow, then an agent. Move up only when the simpler pattern can't handle the variability the task requires.

Over-tooling and under-tooling. Routing behaviour depends on how tools are described and how many are registered. Too many tools with overlapping descriptions produce erratic routing (the more common production problem; teams register everything "just in case"). Too few force the agent to hallucinate a path or return incomplete results. Start with the minimum set and add tools only for a confirmed capability gap.

Multi-agent. A planner, executor and evaluator running as separate agents handing off through structured artifacts introduces additional design decisions beyond the loop; the economics are covered in the evals/cost notes.

Real life. An assembly line (workflow) versus a handyman told "fix the leak" (agent). Use the line when every unit is the same; hire the handyman when each problem is different.

Tech. A cron-driven ETL pipeline versus an on-call engineer debugging an unknown outage.

notes.title: Wiring paths
notes.html:
The pattern is constant; the wiring is a choice. Once you decide a task needs an agent, you have decided on a pattern: a loop that calls tools, manages context and runs until a goal is met. What differs across the three wiring paths is how much of the loop you write yourself versus hand to a library or hosted service. Choose based on deployment and compliance constraints, not on which is fastest to prototype.

Path Who runs the loop What you own Check before committing
Raw Messages API loop your code runs every iteration the full loop, tool execution, context management, retries, exit conditions maintenance cost is yours: everything an SDK would give free (context management, parallel tool handling) becomes code you write and test
Agent SDK the same loop runs inside your own process; the SDK provides the iteration structure, tool registration, system prompt setup and context management tool execution (your code still executes tools), your environment config is code/filesystem-level; settingSources controls what loads
Claude Managed Agents (public beta) Anthropic runs the loop and the sandbox; you define the agent once (model, system prompt, tools, MCP servers, skills), refer to it by ID, send user events and stream results back over SSE an agent definition (a versioned API resource) and an application layer that sends events and consumes the stream beta surface that can change; requires beta header managed-agents-2026-04-01

What Managed Agents lets you stop owning. The iteration loop, the execution sandbox, retries inside the loop and the tool-execution runtime; long-running execution (minutes to hours) without your process holding the loop open; sandbox provisioning and teardown. What you take on: server-side session state (sessions are stored by Anthropic and subject to its data handling), a dependency on the managed sandbox's tools and execution model, an agent-as-resource definition format, and a beta surface.

The constraint that decides it for regulated work. Managed Agent sessions are stateful and stored server-side. That storage is why they are not currently eligible for Zero Data Retention or a HIPAA BAA. If your workload carries PHI or falls under a ZDR requirement, this path is ruled out regardless of operational fit; route to the Agent SDK or a raw loop on a covered configuration. The governing constraint picks the path before convenience gets a say.

Typical progression. Prototype on the Agent SDK locally, then move to Managed Agents for production. Expect a re-expression step (code/filesystem config versus a versioned API resource), not a direct export.

The four loop steps that hold on every path.

  1. Register tools (same schema structure everywhere).
  2. Set the system prompt, scoped to the agent's task. A broad prompt produces broader, less reliable routing; naming the task and its available tools produces consistent behaviour.
  3. Handle the tool-use loop: whichever way the loop is iterated, your code (or the sandbox) executes every call and returns a tool-result block for each.
  4. Define exit conditions: without explicit ones the agent keeps requesting tool calls beyond what the task needs. Define when "done" means done.

Loop wiring checklist (verify on every path). Tools registered and referenced consistently; system prompt scoped (doesn't describe tools the agent lacks; doesn't omit tools that need scoping guidance); every tool-use block from one assistant turn resolved together; at least one human-in-the-loop insertion point defined; exit conditions that don't depend on Claude volunteering to stop.

Real life. Cooking from scratch, using a meal kit, or ordering delivery: each hands off more, and each brings constraints (delivery can't be hospital-sterile).

Tech. Self-hosted Kubernetes, an application framework, or a fully managed PaaS.

notes.title: Human in the loop
notes.html:
What it is. A checkpoint that pauses agent execution and routes to a human review step before proceeding. The governing question: what is the worst possible outcome if this step runs without a human check?

Insertion point What triggers it Risk addressed
Before a destructive tool call the agent is about to execute a write, delete or send High: irreversible actions where a wrong call can't be undone
After a planning step the agent produced a plan and is about to execute it Medium: an incorrect plan that gives the wrong outcome even if every step executes correctly
On unexpected output a tool result has an error flag, is empty, or is outside expected bounds Variable: failure modes that retry logic alone won't resolve

The incident to remember (the config-editing agent). An agent with read_file, write_file and validate_config was tested in a scratch directory and converged in two or three iterations. In a customer environment it corrected an out-of-range rate limit, re-ran validate_config (pass), and the loop exited after one iteration, exactly as designed. The rate limit was one the customer's application depended on; validate_config checked the schema range, not downstream dependencies. The customer's app was throttled within minutes. The loop design was correct; the exit condition was scoped to the file being edited and there was no checkpoint between "validation passed on this file" and "write committed to the customer environment". Fix: before the first live write_file, pause and surface the proposed change for human review — an explicit branch between "proposed change ready" and "write committed".

Why tests missed it. In a disposable test environment a wrong write touches nothing that matters. The design question that was never asked: "What's the worst outcome if write_file runs without a human check?" Register that constraint when scoping the tool surface, not after the first incident.

Distinguish proposing from committing. The gap between an agent that proposes a change and one that commits it is where the checkpoint belongs.

Connection to Claude Code. The same worst-case question places the gate in Claude Code: reversible, low-stakes actions pass without a gate; hard-to-undo actions or sensitive paths get a deterministic deny rule or a prompt; and the agent should never be the only gate on changes to code your team has marked sensitive.

Real life. A surgeon's checklist: the "time-out" happens before the first cut, not after.

Tech. A required human review on changes to production deploy config, however green CI is.

notes.title: Permission modes
notes.html:
Purpose. Permission modes control how often Claude Code stops to ask for confirmation. Each trades speed for oversight; the right choice depends on how well you know the codebase and how reversible the changes are. Claude Code's workflow is explore → plan → code; plan mode holds it in exploration.

Mode Auto-approves Still gates Use for / limits
default reads only nearly every edit and command baseline for new/unfamiliar codebases; safe but slow on trusted work
acceptEdits reads, file edits, and common filesystem commands (mkdir, touch, rm, rmdir, mv, cp, sed) inside the working directory all other shell commands; writes outside the working directory; writes to protected paths trusted local work where shell execution still needs a human eye; not for agents that must run scripts
plan reads only; researches and proposes, no edits all edits and shell commands until you approve a plan exploration/planning on sensitive or unfamiliar code; not for tasks that must write output
auto everything, but a separate classifier reviews each action first and blocks anything escalating beyond your request, targeting unrecognized infrastructure, or driven by hostile/inappropriate content production deploys and migrations, mass deletes, credential exfiltration and force-push to main are blocked by default reduces prompts but doesn't guarantee safety; a research preview; availability depends on plan, model version and admin settings
dontAsk only tools pre-approved in an allow rule, plus read-only commands auto-denies everything else; no confirmation queue locked-down CI and scripts; not a way to reduce friction on interactive work
bypassPermissions all tool calls: no prompts and no safety checks (also skips the protected-path guard) only catastrophic deletes like rm -rf / and rm -rf ~ trigger a last-resort prompt only inside an isolated container/VM where the environment is disposable; never a workstation against a live codebase

The bypass incident. A developer switched to bypassPermissions to rename old API endpoint references. A cleanup script matched /v1/legacy/ in both /src/ and /deploy/config/prod/ and deleted three production config files with no prompt. In default or acceptEdits the script invocation would have prompted (note: acceptEdits auto-approves direct rm inside the working directory, so only default mode would prompt for direct deletions). Lessons: the failure pattern is an over-broad match in a mode with no checkpoints; set deny rules on sensitive directories before switching modes; if you want fewer prompts without losing a net, use the classifier-gated auto instead of a full bypass.

Costs, complexity, risk. Default mode adds prompt latency to every call (accumulating on long refactors). Multiple settings levels with an override hierarchy need consistent care. The risk is using the wrong mode for the context.

Real life. Driving modes: learner (default), your own street (acceptEdits), a satnav preview (plan), cruise control with lane assist (auto), a locked company fleet car (dontAsk), a racetrack (bypass).

notes.title: Settings hierarchy
notes.html:
Where configuration lives and who it applies to. Settings can sit at several levels; each level defines the scope of the rules it contains.

Level Location Applies to Right place for
User ~/.claude/settings.json every project on the machine preferences that follow you (e.g. a preferred default mode)
Project .claude/settings.json (committed) everyone who clones the repo team conventions; allow rules for project tools; deny rules for paths that shouldn't be touched
Local project .claude/settings.local.json (auto git-ignored) you, in this project personal overrides that shouldn't be committed
Enterprise/managed managed-settings.json (set by admins) everyone; cannot be overridden by users or project files org-wide security: deny edits to env files, block specific shell commands across all projects

Allow/deny rules layer on top of the chosen mode, and a deny rule always wins over an allow rule, regardless of mode. The most durable governance control is an enterprise-level deny rule: no individual developer can remove it and it applies even when a bypass mode is set. A conflict between an enterprise deny and a project allow must be understood by everyone maintaining the config.

Where a human must still look. Modes and deny rules decide what the agent can do without asking; the review gate decides where a person must look before an action lands. Same worst-case question: let low-stakes reversible actions through (what acceptEdits is for); gate actions that are hard to undo or reach sensitive paths (writes outside the working dir, destructive commands, edits to security-relevant files — enforce deterministically with a deny rule, keep the prompt with default/plan mode); never let the agent be the only gate on changes to sensitive code (also true for unattended automations such as a bot blocking PRs).

Real life. House rules, building rules, city law. You can't opt out of city law.

Tech. Team ESLint config versus an org-wide policy-as-code enforcement.

notes.title: CLAUDE.md, rules and hooks
notes.html:
Three mechanisms with different guarantees. This is configuration of what the agent knows and how it behaves, as opposed to what it's allowed to do.

CLAUDE.md. On start in a project directory Claude Code reads CLAUDE.md at the root; its contents are appended to your prompt before any message arrives, so every convention is present from the first prompt of every session. /init scans the codebase and generates a starter file — a baseline you must validate and refine toward the rules that control outcomes: test commands, framework conventions, paths not to touch, style choices that differ from defaults.

  • Size is the main failure mode. A larger file consumes more context and makes any single instruction a smaller fraction of what loads, reducing the chance the one critical rule is followed. In the incident, an 847-line CLAUDE.md (framework prefs, style guide, dependency rules, a historical decisions log, archived notes) had a path restriction on line 347; the agent edited the forbidden directory anyway. The rule was present; dilution defeated it.
  • Keep CLAUDE.md to constraints that change behaviour; move the rest to Skills (on demand), rules files, or reference docs read on demand. The one rule you can't afford to dilute should be the shortest path to a hook.

Rules files (.claude/rules/). Narrow, path-specific guidance. Scope comes from a paths glob in the YAML frontmatter:

---
paths:
  - "src/db/**/*.sql"
---
All SQL in the database module must include an explicit transaction boundary.

A scoped rule enters context only when Claude works with matching files. Scoping comes from the frontmatter, not file placement: subdirectories (e.g. .claude/rules/database/) are organizational only; a rules file without paths loads unconditionally at launch, like CLAUDE.md, wherever it sits.

Hooks. Scripts that intercept and control tool calls at lifecycle events, configured in settings (and via /hooks): an event, an optional matcher scoping to tool types, and a command. A CLAUDE.md line "run Prettier after every edit" is followed most of the time; a hook makes it happen every time because it fires independently of the model's decision. Core events:

  • PreToolUse: before a tool call; can examine it and exit with code 2 to block, with the reason on stderr as feedback the agent sees. This is how access control is enforced at the configuration layer.
  • PostToolUse: after a call completes; cannot block (it already happened); use for formatters, tests, audit logging.
  • UserPromptSubmit: when you submit a prompt, before processing (inject context / validate).
  • Stop: when the model finishes responding (notifications, cleanup, committing an audit log).
  • Notification: when Claude needs permission or after 60 seconds idle.
  • SessionStart / SessionEnd: initialize/validate and teardown/final audit. A PreToolUse hook blocking edits to a production config path enforces the constraint at every tool call in every session regardless of permission mode: the difference between a guardrail and a convention.

Mechanism map.

Mechanism Loads Cost Belongs here
CLAUDE.md every session persistent; dilutes with size universal constraints, commands, framework decisions
Rules file paths-scoped on matching files; unscoped at launch only when triggered (scoped) path-specific guidance
Hook runs your script at an event; no content added minimal enforced guardrails, side effects, audit logging
Subagent task context only, isolated returns a summary exploration, noisy or parallelizable work

Real life. A sign saying "please don't walk on the grass" (CLAUDE.md) versus a locked gate (hook).

Tech. A style guide in the wiki versus a pre-commit hook that rejects the commit.

notes.title: Subagents and plugins
notes.html:
Subagents. A specialized assistant Claude Code delegates to; each runs a task in its own isolated context and returns only its output. It starts from a clean slate: no inherited conversation history, accumulated files or session state, and no skills (it does inherit the parent's permission context). Built-ins differ in what they load:

  • Explore and Plan skip CLAUDE.md and git status to keep research fast and cheap, so project rules defined in CLAUDE.md are not in their context.
  • The general-purpose subagent loads both. If project constraints must be respected, use the general-purpose subagent or a custom subagent (in .claude/agents) that explicitly loads the rules it needs. A custom subagent that needs a skill must list that skill explicitly in its frontmatter; built-ins have none preloaded, so skill-backed behaviour in a built-in agent means creating a custom subagent with skills listed. Check the current built-in list in the docs since it evolves.

Skills, commands, plugins: three packaging layers.

Layer What For Reach for it when
Skill SKILL.md in .claude/skills, loaded when the description matches or by name an individual or team using Claude Code interactively a task-specific procedure should stay out of context until needed (PR review, deploy checklist)
Custom command a named shortcut for an explicit procedure developers wanting a predictable entry point high-frequency procedures with a clear name triggered directly
Plugin a versioned bundle of skills, hooks, subagents and MCP servers distributed via a marketplace a team wanting one-step installation of a shared, versioned setup a working setup lives on one machine and must be shared and kept consistent

In current Claude Code, skills are the recommended format for both explicit and automatic invocation: /skill-name directly or loaded automatically when relevant; add disable-model-invocation: true in the frontmatter for a workflow that runs only when called explicitly. The older .claude/commands/ format still works but is legacy.

Plugin details.

  • Plugin commands are namespaced by plugin name: run-tests in a plugin named payments is /payments:run-tests, so two plugins can both ship run-tests. The plugin name is part of the interface; renaming renames every command.
  • The official Anthropic marketplace is available automatically; add third-party marketplaces (a GitHub repo) with /plugin marketplace add <owner/repo>; teammates then run one install command.
  • Enterprise: admins can deploy plugins organization-wide via managed settings; a managed marketplace allowlist gates which sources users may add but does not register marketplaces; pair it with extraKnownMarketplaces to push one to all users. Managed scope sits above user and project settings so it can't be overridden.
  • Portability trap: a plugin that hard-codes absolute paths or environment assumptions installs fine for the author and fails for everyone else.
  • Cost: skills add context on activation; a plugin adds install and maintenance overhead — pay the setup cost once (plugin) versus repeatedly (every developer repeating manual steps).

Skills across runtimes (Claude Code / Messages API / Agent SDK / Managed Agents) is covered in the context notes; the portability rules: description as matching criterion, no local-environment assumptions, subagents don't inherit skills.

Real life. Hiring a contractor who hasn't read your house rules (subagent) versus a starter kit handed to every new tenant (plugin).

Tech. A worker process with a fresh environment; an npm package bundling config.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
Workflow vs agent. Enumerable steps, real error cost, standard observability → workflow; unenumerable path, goal + tools → agent. Ladder: single call → workflow → agent. Over-tooling degrades routing; under-tooling forces hallucinated paths.

Wiring paths. Raw loop (full control/maintenance), Agent SDK (loop in your process; you execute tools), Managed Agents (Anthropic runs loop and sandbox; agent as versioned resource; sessions stored server-side → no ZDR/HIPAA BAA; beta header managed-agents-2026-04-01). Four loop steps: register tools, scope system prompt, handle tool_use, define exit conditions that don't rely on Claude stopping.

HITL. Ask the worst-case question. Gate before destructive calls (high), after plans (medium), on unexpected output (variable). A validator passing on one file isn't a downstream-impact check; separate proposing from committing.

Permission modes. default, acceptEdits (working-dir edits + common fs commands), plan, auto (classifier-gated, research preview), dontAsk (allow-list or deny; CI), bypassPermissions (no checks, containers only). Set deny rules before switching modes; prefer auto over bypass.

Settings. User, project, local, enterprise managed (non-overridable). Deny beats allow in every mode; enterprise deny is the most durable control.

CLAUDE.md/rules/hooks. CLAUDE.md always loads and dilutes with size (847-line failure); rules scoped by paths frontmatter (unscoped = launch-time); hooks enforce deterministically (PreToolUse exit 2 blocks; PostToolUse can't block; plus UserPromptSubmit, Stop, Notification, SessionStart/End).

Subagents/plugins. Subagents: isolated, no history, no skills, inherit permissions; Explore/Plan skip CLAUDE.md. Plugins bundle skills/hooks/subagents/MCP; namespaced commands; marketplaces; managed allowlist + extraKnownMarketplaces; avoid absolute paths.

One-liners.

  • "Climb the ladder only as far as the variability demands."
  • "The governing constraint picks the wiring path."
  • "Gate by worst case, enforce with deny rules and hooks."
  • "A hook is a guardrail; CLAUDE.md is a convention."

questions.promptHtml:
A task always follows the same five steps and inputs are well constrained. What should you build?

  • A. An agent, for flexibility
  • B. A workflow, because you can enumerate the steps in code
  • C. A multi-agent orchestrator
  • D. Nothing; it cannot be automated

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Start with the simplest pattern: single call, then workflow, then agent only if the path cannot be enumerated.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Agents add behavioral complexity and transcript-level observability needs. Choose an agent when you can specify the goal and tools but not the path, and inputs vary unpredictably.

questions.promptHtml:
A healthcare product handles PHI and needs a long-running agent. A teammate suggests Claude Managed Agents because it removes the loop and sandbox work. What is the problem?

  • A. Managed Agents cannot call tools
  • B. Managed Agent sessions are stateful and stored server-side, so they are not currently eligible for Zero Data Retention or a HIPAA BAA; use the Agent SDK or a raw loop on a covered configuration
  • C. Managed Agents only run for seconds
  • D. There is no problem; BAAs cover beta features

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. The governing compliance constraint picks the wiring path before convenience does.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Three paths: raw Messages API loop (you own everything), Agent SDK (runs the loop in your process; you still execute tools), Managed Agents (public beta; Anthropic runs the loop and sandbox; agent defined as a versioned API resource; beta header managed-agents-2026-04-01). A BAA also excludes Console, Workbench, beta features and consumer plans.

questions.contextHtml: A config-editing agent (read_file, write_file, validate_config) was tested in a scratch directory. In a customer environment it corrected an out-of-range rate limit, validate_config passed, the loop exited. Minutes later the customer's app was throttled and failing.
questions.promptHtml:
What design step was missing?

  • A. More loop iterations
  • B. A checkpoint between "proposed change ready" and "write committed", placed by asking the worst outcome if write_file runs unchecked
  • C. A stricter schema for validate_config
  • D. Lower temperature

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Blaming the validator or the loop cap.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What depends on that value downstream? Is the environment reversible?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Restore the old value.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Missing HITL gate; validator too narrow; exit condition too narrow.
  4. How I'd verify each: Review the exit condition and the tool's blast radius.
  5. Root cause: Exit condition scoped to the file; no gate before a production write.
  6. Fix: Pause and surface proposed changes for human approval before the first live write (or a PreToolUse hook); keep a dry-run mode.
  7. Prevention: Ask the worst-case question during tool scoping, not after the first incident.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not gate every read; reserve gates for irreversible actions.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html: • Other insertion points? → After a planning step (wrong plan), and on unexpected output (error, empty, out-of-bounds).

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tunes the loop.
  • Hire: adds approval.
  • Strong hire: places gates by worst-case cost and enforces with a hook.

questions.promptHtml:
Which mode is built for locked-down CI where anything not pre-approved must be refused with no prompt queue?

  • A. acceptEdits
  • B. plan
  • C. dontAsk
  • D. bypassPermissions

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: C. dontAsk auto-approves only allow-listed tools plus read-only commands and auto-denies the rest.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: default prompts on edits and commands; acceptEdits allows edits and common filesystem commands (mkdir touch rm rmdir mv cp sed) inside the working directory; plan blocks edits and commands until a plan is approved; auto lets a classifier review each action and blocks risky ones (research preview); bypassPermissions skips all prompts and the protected-path guard and is only for disposable containers or VMs.

questions.contextHtml: A developer switched to bypassPermissions to rename /v1/legacy/ endpoint references. A cleanup script matched the same pattern in /deploy/config/prod/ and deleted three files with no prompt.
questions.promptHtml:
What should have been done?

  • A. Nothing; this was unforeseeable
  • B. Set deny rules on sensitive directories first, and use auto (classifier-gated) or default/acceptEdits instead of a full bypass
  • C. Trust the agent more
  • D. Run the script in plan mode

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Treating it as a model bug instead of a configuration choice.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Was the pattern anchored to /src/? Was an enterprise deny rule set?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Restore from version control or backups.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Over-broad glob; no deny rule; bypass mode.
  4. How I'd verify each: Replay the match in a dry run.
  5. Root cause: Over-broad pattern plus a mode with no checkpoints.
  6. Fix: B. Note the gate would have been the script invocation prompt in default mode.
  7. Prevention: Enterprise deny rule on /deploy/config/**; deny always beats allow.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not use bypass on a workstation against a live codebase.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html: • Would acceptEdits have stopped direct rm in the working dir? → No, it auto-approves rm inside the working directory.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the agent.
  • Hire: sets deny rules.
  • Strong hire: explains where the gate sat and chooses auto plus enterprise deny.

questions.promptHtml:
An administrator needs a rule denying edits to .env files that no developer or project file can override. Where does it go?

  • A. ~/.claude/settings.json
  • B. .claude/settings.json in the repo
  • C. .claude/settings.local.json
  • D. Enterprise managed-settings.json

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: D. Managed settings sit above user and project scope and cannot be overridden; deny beats allow in every mode.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Scope order is user, project, local project, then enterprise managed settings; managed sits on top and cannot be overridden by users or project files. A deny rule always beats an allow rule regardless of mode, so an enterprise deny is the most durable governance control. User, project and local files are all editable by developers or the repo.

questions.promptHtml:
"Run the formatter after every edit" and "never touch /legacy/tokens/" must hold every single time. How should each be enforced?

  • A. Write both in CLAUDE.md
  • B. A PostToolUse hook for the formatter and a PreToolUse hook (exit code 2) or deny rule for the protected path
  • C. A longer system prompt
  • D. A subagent

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Hooks run independently of the model's decision; CLAUDE.md is a suggestion that dilutes as it grows.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: PreToolUse can block (exit 2, reason on stderr); PostToolUse cannot block, which suits formatters, tests and audit logging. Others: UserPromptSubmit, Stop, Notification, SessionStart, SessionEnd. In an incident an 847-line CLAUDE.md let a one-line path restriction get ignored by dilution; keep CLAUDE.md to behavior-changing rules and path-scope the rest with .claude/rules/ using a paths glob (a rule without paths loads at launch like CLAUDE.md, regardless of folder).

questions.promptHtml:
You delegate a refactor to the built-in Explore subagent expecting it to respect your CLAUDE.md conventions. It does not. Why?

  • A. CLAUDE.md is ignored everywhere
  • B. Explore and Plan skip CLAUDE.md and git status for speed; use the general-purpose subagent or a custom subagent that loads the rules
  • C. Subagents inherit skills automatically
  • D. Subagents share the parent's full history

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Subagents start clean; only the general-purpose one loads CLAUDE.md, and custom ones need skills listed explicitly.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Subagents start from a clean slate and do not inherit conversation history or skills (they do inherit the parent's permission context). Explore and Plan skip CLAUDE.md and git status to stay fast and cheap; the general-purpose subagent loads both. For work that must respect project rules, use general-purpose or a custom subagent in .claude/agents that lists the skills and rules it needs.

questions.promptHtml:
A plugin named payments ships a run-tests command. How is it invoked, and what is the portability risk?

  • A. /run-tests; no risk
  • B. /payments:run-tests; hard-coded absolute paths or environment assumptions will work for the author and fail on other machines
  • C. /plugin run-tests; plugins cannot be shared
  • D. /payments/run-tests; plugin names don't matter

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Plugin commands are namespaced by plugin name, so renaming the plugin renames every command.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: A plugin bundles skills, hooks, subagents and MCP servers, distributed through a marketplace (/plugin marketplace add <owner/repo>). Enterprise admins gate sources with a managed allowlist and push one with extraKnownMarketplaces. Skills are now the recommended format; disable-model-invocation: true makes a skill explicit-only; .claude/commands/ is legacy.

questions.promptHtml:
User inputs vary wildly and the path to the goal cannot be listed in advance. What fits?

  • A. A fixed workflow
  • B. An agent given a goal and tools
  • C. A single prompt with no tools
  • D. A cron job

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Unenumerable paths are the case for agents; accept non-determinism and add transcript-level observability.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Climb only as needed: single call, then workflow, then agent.

questions.promptHtml:
Why must a loop have exit conditions that do not depend on Claude deciding to stop?

  • A. Claude cannot stop
  • B. Without them the agent may keep requesting tool calls beyond what the task needs
  • C. The API requires it
  • D. It improves caching

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Define when "done" means done (max iterations, success predicate).

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: The four loop steps are: register tools, scope the system prompt, handle every tool_use, define exit conditions.

questions.promptHtml:
What does Claude Managed Agents take off your plate?

  • A. Model selection
  • B. The iteration loop, the sandbox and tool-execution runtime, run by Anthropic server-side
  • C. Your prompts
  • D. Your evals

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. In exchange, sessions are stored server-side and it is a beta surface that can change.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: It needs the managed-agents-2026-04-01 beta header. Skills are attached to the agent definition, not at session time.

questions.promptHtml:
A team registers 60 tools "just in case" and tool selection gets erratic. Fix?

  • A. Add 20 more descriptions
  • B. Start with the minimum tool set and add tools only when a specific capability gap is confirmed
  • C. Lower the temperature
  • D. Switch to streaming

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Selection quality degrades as the tool surface grows.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Too few tools is the opposite failure: the agent hallucinates a path or returns incomplete results.

questions.promptHtml:
Which is true of acceptEdits?

  • A. It auto-approves all shell commands
  • B. It auto-approves edits and common filesystem commands inside the working directory; other shell commands and protected paths still prompt
  • C. It blocks all edits
  • D. It disables deny rules

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. It is scoped to paths inside the working directory.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Deny rules still win. It is not appropriate if the agent must run arbitrary scripts.

questions.promptHtml:
How does auto differ from bypassPermissions?

  • A. They are identical
  • B. auto has a separate classifier review each action and block risky ones; bypass has no checks at all
  • C. auto only reads files
  • D. bypass uses a classifier

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Want fewer prompts without losing the safety net? Use a classifier-gated mode.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: auto is a research preview and not a substitute for reviewing sensitive operations.

questions.promptHtml:
Project settings allow editing config/, enterprise settings deny it. What happens?

  • A. The project allow wins
  • B. The deny wins; deny beats allow in every mode and managed settings cannot be overridden
  • C. The user is prompted every time
  • D. The most recent file wins

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. The most durable governance control is an enterprise deny rule.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: The reasoning and a real-world analogy are in the master notes section "settings hierarchy". Use the Source button to jump there.

questions.promptHtml:
What can a PostToolUse hook NOT do?

  • A. Run a formatter
  • B. Block the tool call that just completed
  • C. Write an audit log
  • D. Trigger tests

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. The call has already happened; blocking belongs in PreToolUse.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: PreToolUse can exit with code 2 and write the reason to stderr as feedback the agent sees.

questions.promptHtml:
A rules file in .claude/rules/database/ has no paths frontmatter. When does it load?

  • A. Only when database files are touched
  • B. At launch, unconditionally, like CLAUDE.md; folder placement is organizational only
  • C. Never
  • D. Only in plan mode

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Scoping comes from the paths glob, not from the folder.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: The reasoning and a real-world analogy are in the master notes section "claude md rules and hooks". Use the Source button to jump there.

questions.promptHtml:
Admins want a marketplace pushed to everyone and sources restricted. What do they use?

  • A. Individual user settings
  • B. A managed allowlist for sources plus extraKnownMarketplaces in managed settings to register it
  • C. A README
  • D. A hook

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. The allowlist alone only restricts what users may add; it does not register a marketplace.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Managed scope sits above user and project settings, so users cannot override it.
